query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin, conformal high‐entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer onto the tungsten features during spark plasma sintering will suppress phase separation and eliminate interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity under coupled heat‐transfer and irradiation conditions typical of plasma‐facing/cooling joint applications. This improvement is achieved through a multicomponent mixing effect that promotes sluggish diffusion at the interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite in which tungsten exists as discrete particles or an interconnected ligament network embedded in a copper matrix that exhibits phase separation and the formation of interfacial voids under processing and service conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a single processing step that deposits a thin HEA interlayer (e.g., one based on refractory elements such as (CrFeTiTa)70W30 or VFeTiTaW) on the tungsten surfaces/interfaces during spark plasma sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing should be conducted via spark plasma sintering at temperatures that promote localized in situ formation of the HEA interlayer without excessive interdiffusion; the service environment involves high heat flux and irradiation conditions as encountered in joints between W‐based plasma‐facing components and Cu‐based cooling systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, conformal HEA interlayer at the W/Cu interface that acts as a diffusion barrier and stress-mediator, ensuring improved interfacial bonding and continuity.
generation.mechanism: The HEA interlayer, owing to its high configurational entropy, promotes a multicomponent mixing effect characterized by sluggish diffusion at the interface, which minimizes lattice mismatch and thermal expansion disparities, thereby preventing void nucleation and phase separation even under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated composite, the HEA-interlayer-modified composite is expected to show significantly reduced interfacial voids and phase separation, leading to enhanced thermal conductivity under in-service thermal and irradiation stresses.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites typically develop phase segregations and voids at the tungsten-copper interfaces, degrading their thermal transport properties under high heat flux and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to composites fabricated by spark plasma sintering with controlled deposition of HEA interlayers. Its effectiveness is anticipated to hold in the irradiation and heat flux ranges relevant to fusion reactor joint conditions, although the exact quantitative benefit may depend on processing optimization and HEA composition.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement is supported by evidence on HEA-induced thermal and irradiation stability in refractory systems, the precise enhancement in thermal conductivity and long-term interface stability requires further quantitative evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples via spark plasma sintering: one set with the in situ deposited HEA interlayer (e.g., using a refractory HEA composition) and one set without. Expose both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and irradiation (using He+ or relevant ions) that mimic fusion service conditions. Then, evaluate their interfacial microstructures (via SEM/TEM) and measure thermal conductivity.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of interfacial void density and phase separation (SEM/TEM)
Thermal conductivity tests under controlled heat flux
Irradiation-induced microstructural changes and bonding integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the HEA interlayer do not show statistically significant reductions in interfacial voids and phase separation, nor exhibit improved thermal conductivity relative to the untreated samples under both accelerated thermal and irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. Both (as-sintered) alloys were irradiated with Ar+ (150 keV) with a fluence of 2.4 × 1020 at/m2, as well as He+ (10 keV) and D+ (5 keV) both with a fluence of 5 × 1021 at/m2. Th

Previous studies on (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys have already demonstrated notable mechanical properties as candidates for the thermal barrier interlayer []; for example, showing a ductile behavior strain–-stress magnitude of around 300 MPa for vanadium and around 400 MPa for chromium-based alloys, exhibited at 1000 °C. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of knowledge on thermal stability at higher temperatures and irradiation resistance, which are important aspects to consider for the behavior of the materials subject to extreme environments, especially nuclear fusion. Refractory, low activation high-entropy alloys such as TiVCrTa [], TiVCrFeMn [], and (CrVTiTa)1−xWx [], where x is the atomic fraction (0.3 to 0.9), have been proposed for nuclear applications. This class of alloys is particularly promising as a thermal barrier interlayer due to its high thermal stability [] and high temperature strength [,], as well as high radiation resistance [] and low thermal diffusivity []. Based on this, the study of refractory alloys was pursued based on W, since it is the chosen plasma-facing component. This work presents the production of entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys

The WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloy with 32at.% of tungsten (W) and its derivative alloys with 42 to 90at.% of W with in-situ TiC were prepared via the mixing of elemental W, Ta, Ti, V and Cr powders followed by spark plasma sintering for the development of reduced-activation alloys for fusion plasma-facing materials. Characterization of the sintered samples revealed a BCC lattice and a multi-phase structure. The selected-area diffraction patterns confirmed the formation of TiC in the high-entropy alloy and its derivative alloys. It revealed the development of C15 (cubic) Laves phases as well in alloys with 71 to 90at.% W. A mechanical examination of the samples revealed a more than twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening. This study explored the potential of powder metallurgy processing for the fabrication of a high-entropy alloy and other derived compositions with enhanced hardness and strength.
